summary:
New Caledonia is a French collectivity in which France retains responsibility for penal law, civil-status documents and the justice system, while New Caledonia legislates locally on many domestic matters. The protections a trans visitor would rely on are French national provisions that apply here as French law, and no source in this inventory records a local ordinance narrowing them. Nothing in the inventory criminalises trans people or same-sex relations.

Same-sex marriage has been available in New Caledonia since France's 2013 marriage-equality statute, which applies here as French law. CNN reported on 29 May 2013 on the first same-sex wedding solemnised in France under that law. PinkNews reported on 26 August 2012 that the French government would introduce its same-sex marriage and adoption bill into Parliament in October 2012, fulfilling President Hollande's campaign pledge.

Sexual identity became a ground of discrimination in the French Penal Code through the sexual-harassment legislation of 2012, which enabled prosecution of discrimination and of transphobia as discrimination. Yagg reported that change in July 2012; the provision was amended in 2016 to read gender identity. As French law, the provision reaches New Caledonia.

Placement of detainees follows the recorded legal gender marker rather than anatomy. Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code assigns incarcerated trans people according to their recorded sex, which in practice puts trans women in all-male facilities where they face threats of assault by other detainees. BuzzFeed News reported that practice on 12 January 2018. The French prison framework governs the collectivity's establishments in the same way.

France's detention-places watchdog, the CGLPL, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding a persistence of serious violations of the rights of transgender detainees across all French places of deprivation of liberty. Its findings rest on referrals made since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on inspections at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse, where eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed. Because French law applies here, the opinion extends to establishments in New Caledonia.
tangentialFactors:
The protections recorded for New Caledonia are inherited rather than locally enacted. Marriage equality and the discrimination ground reached the collectivity because France legislated them, not because New Caledonia's own legislature adopted them, so a visitor's recourse rests on French legal machinery rather than on local ordinances.

The detention evidence in this inventory is drawn entirely from mainland France. BuzzFeed News reporting and the CGLPL's 2021 opinion describe conditions at French facilities and in French places of deprivation of liberty; the inference that they govern New Caledonia rests on the extension of French prison law, not on inspection findings made in the collectivity.

The CGLPL opinion treats the mistreatment of transgender detainees as systemic rather than isolated, covering all French places of deprivation of liberty and drawing on referrals accumulated since 2010. That is a materially different posture from the civil-status side of the record, where the inventory shows recognition and marriage access without any recorded local restriction.

The wording of the anti-discrimination ground shifted in 2016 from sexual identity to gender identity, so documentation dated before that year may describe the protection in narrower terms than the provision now carries.
localsOnly:
Residents of New Caledonia live under the same French prison framework that governs establishments in the collectivity, including the Article D248 rule that assigns detainees by recorded legal sex rather than by anatomy.

The Penal Code discrimination ground covering gender identity applies to residents as it does to visitors, and transphobic conduct is prosecutable as discrimination under that provision.

Same-sex marriage for residents rests on the French 2013 statute rather than on a local enactment, so changes to French national law would travel to New Caledonia without a local vote.

New Caledonia legislates locally on many domestic matters, but the inventory records no local ordinance on gender recognition, detention or anti-discrimination that departs from the French national position.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses how a trans visitor's documents are examined on arrival in New Caledonia, whether entry or visa screening records gender markers, or which authorities perform those checks. Entry and screening risk is unresolved here, not absent.

The inventory contains no account of a gender-recognition procedure available in New Caledonia specifically, and no source describing how a marker change made in France is reflected on documents used in the collectivity.

The CGLPL's 2021 opinion covers French places of deprivation of liberty on the basis of referrals and inspections conducted in mainland France. Whether the same watchdog has inspected establishments in New Caledonia, and what it found there, is unresolved from these sources.

No source in the inventory records a hate-crime statute that names gender identity as an aggravating factor, and no source records enforcement outcomes for the discrimination provision in New Caledonia. Whether courts in the collectivity have charged transphobic conduct as discrimination is unverified here.

Healthcare access for trans people in New Caledonia, including whether treatment begun in France continues without interruption, is not covered by any source in this inventory.
